question: Can group-sparse PDE discovery with stability selection turn stochastic active-particle trajectories into physically consistent deterministic hydrodynamic equations, including density-dependent coefficients and hidden forcing fields, and do the paper's support-recovery, simulation, and artifact checks validate the learned continuum models beyond the hand-designed libraries and source simulations?

key_findings.claim: The paper's defensible novelty is a cross-scale active-matter application of an existing group-sparse PDE-discovery stack, not the first particle-to-hydrodynamic learning method or the invention of stability-selected group sparsity.
key_findings.evidence: The pipeline combines adaptive coarse-graining of particle trajectories, a manually specified PDE dictionary, group iterative hard thresholding, stability selection, and post-hoc smoothness regression. PDE-FIND, parametric group-sparse PDE discovery, PDE-STRIDE, and the authors' own 2020 group-sparsity framework already supplied the core inference machinery. Supekar et al. had already learned active-matter hydrodynamic equations directly from particle simulations and experiments with symmetry-aware sparse regression. The narrower contribution is applying group support priors to three stochastic particle systems and demonstrating variable coefficients and a latent field in that setting.

key_findings.claim: The method is a transparent five-stage pipeline, but every stage embeds consequential modeling choices.
key_findings.evidence: Particle positions, velocities, or orientations are smoothed into density, polarity, or velocity fields; their time derivative and candidate spatial terms form a regression system; non-overlapping groups encode conservation, symmetry, shared support, variable coefficients, or latent fields; a nonconvex group-L0 problem is approximately solved across a regularization path; repeated half-sample selection chooses stable supports, followed by least-squares or trend-filtered coefficient estimation and PDE simulation. This modular structure is useful, but results inherit the chosen fields, kernel bandwidth, derivatives, candidate terms, grouping, threshold, and solver behavior.

anchors.section: Supplement I / adaptive KDE and dictionaries
Supplement II / Figure 1 and stability selection
Supplement III / grouping and smoothness regression

key_findings.claim: Physical consistency is supplied by the analyst's dictionary and grouping, not guaranteed by sparse regression itself.
key_findings.evidence: The scalar library is manually restricted to flux divergences and selected polynomials; the vector library hard-codes 14 symmetry-compatible terms, including those motivated by known active-matter models. The hidden-field experiment explicitly appends the correct classes of products with an unknown gradient field. Grouping can preserve a user-specified conservation or symmetry relation, but it cannot detect a missing relevant term, an incorrect coarse variable, a wrong closure class, or an ill-posed PDE. Indeed, one learned cell model is numerically unstable despite high selection stability.

anchors.section: Cell-model stability discussion and PBP latent-field library

key_findings.claim: Stability selection measures reproducibility under the paper's resampling procedure, not probability that the selected PDE is physically true.
key_findings.evidence: A term's importance is its frequency under random half-samples, and recovery probability is defined relative to an already identified support S-star. For each replicate, success can occur at any lambda on the path. Thus the curves answer whether the algorithm can rediscover its chosen support somewhere along a searched path, not whether that support is the unique continuum law, predicts unseen regimes, or converges to ground truth. Multiple statistically exchangeable terms are explicitly observed in the SPP example.

key_findings.claim: The advertised false-positive control is conditional on stability-selection assumptions that the paper does not verify for correlated space-time samples.
key_findings.evidence: The method repeatedly samples individual rows from coarse-grained fields, even though neighboring points and times share particles, KDE kernels, derivative stencils, and dynamics. Dictionary columns are also strongly correlated, as the paper's own convective-term exchangeability example shows. Classical stability-selection error bounds require assumptions such as exchangeability and a well-defined selection procedure; the paper neither uses blocked independent trajectories nor tests bound calibration. Colored Efp regions should therefore be read as nominal control under an adopted formula, not an empirical guarantee of the actual number of false PDE terms.

key_findings.claim: Near the Vicsek limit, the SPP experiment recovers a continuity equation and two sufficient polarization models, while failing to identify the full kinetic-theory support.
key_findings.evidence: With 3,000 particles, a 10-term density library, and a 14-term polarity library, the density support contains divergence of polarization with coefficient approximating particle speed. Two polarization supports S1,w and S2,w are stable; the larger includes linear and cubic alignment terms. The fuller analytical support SA,w cannot be recovered without lowering the selection threshold or accepting more false positives because one convective term is exchangeable with alternatives on the observed data. This is evidence for a simpler predictive closure, not recovery of the unique kinetic equation.

anchors.section: Supplement Figure 3 and SPP simulation details

key_findings.claim: The SPP lane validation shows one learned closure reproducing a selected pattern speed, but it does not establish parameter-universal hydrodynamics.
key_findings.evidence: The paper simulates S1,rho plus S2,w from the same initial density and parameter setting used to generate the particle data; it reproduces moving density stripes and an average speed near 2.1, whereas the sparser S1,w closure does not produce stripes. No independent initial-condition ensemble, phase diagram, held-out microscopic parameter sweep, uncertainty interval, or long-horizon field error is reported. The result is a valuable sufficiency test at one regime, not universality across active-particle phases.

key_findings.claim: Density-dependent motility is inferred only after the analyst supplies density binning, shared support, and smoothness structure.
key_findings.evidence: For non-negligible crowding, a generic constant-coefficient dictionary is declared ill posed. The remedy partitions space-time locations into manually tolerance-binned density blocks and groups corresponding candidate columns, asserting that the same term remains active while its coefficient varies with density. This recovers the known exponential speed-density curve with small plotted MSE at three gamma values. The method estimates the constitutive curve within the supplied dependency class; it does not discover that density is the relevant covariate among arbitrary hidden particle properties.

key_findings.claim: The epithelial-tissue result is learned from a calibrated stochastic particle simulation, not from epithelial measurement trajectories.
key_findings.evidence: Four thousand simulated cells interact through a specified potential, alignment, friction, and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck forcing whose parameters were previously chosen to reproduce experimental velocity statistics. The regression then learns a deterministic PDE from this synthetic simulation. Calling it a continuum description of cell dynamics in epithelial tissues is directionally reasonable, but the paper contains no direct cell-imaging input, biological holdout, intervention, or validation on a second tissue dataset.

key_findings.claim: The cell-model damping discussion has two direct text-table contradictions, including a coefficient sign that reverses the claimed stabilizing physics.
key_findings.evidence: The paragraph first says S2,u has better recovery and 'this model lacks' u|u| squared, even though Table II assigns that term to S2,u and not S1,u. It later says S2,u is more stable precisely because it contains that damping term. Supplementary Table II prints its coefficient as positive 8e-3 while the linear coefficient is positive 2.7; for a spatially uniform mode, both terms drive growth and a positive cubic cannot saturate the amplitude. The official TeX source contains a commented simulation line with the physically consistent value -0.008, confirming that the rendered table lost a minus sign.

key_findings.claim: Cell-model validation is restricted to same-regime summary statistics and does not test predictive fields or transfer.
key_findings.evidence: The learned PDE is initialized from the coarse-grained particle simulation and compared with that simulator using the marginal velocity-magnitude distribution, power spectrum, and velocity correlation function. Figure 3 shows one set of curves, with no independent seeds or confidence bands for these metrics, no pointwise trajectory forecast, no density dynamics, no held-out initial conditions, and no parameter or geometry shift. High-wavenumber differences occur near the KDE bandwidth cutoff. Agreement supports selected stationary statistics, not a uniquely correct or broadly predictive closure.

anchors.section: Supplement cell initial conditions and coefficients

key_findings.claim: The phoretic-field task reconstructs one smooth deterministic forcing with a hand-designed latent-gradient library; it does not infer an arbitrary stochastic drift field.
key_findings.evidence: The withheld c(x,y) is a sum of 20 sinusoidal products whose wavenumbers are only one or two, while the particle orientations are stochastic. The library is explicitly expanded with symmetry-compatible products of an unknown gradient field, then a 2D Laplacian trend penalty with lambda_f=1 is applied. Only one field, beta=0.3, 5,000 particles, and total time five are tested. The hidden field is deterministic and deliberately smooth, so the abstract's phrase latent stochastic drift fields is broader than the demonstrated task.

key_findings.claim: The reported phoretic 'RMSE' is a squared relative error, making the visual closeness claim numerically ambiguous.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 4 defines its quantity as the ratio of squared L2 norms, ||gradient c minus estimated gradient c|| squared divided by ||gradient c|| squared, and reports 0.2654 while calling it Relative Mean Squared Error and RMSE. The displayed statistic is a normalized squared error; its corresponding relative L2 error is sqrt(0.2654), about 0.515. The unsmoothed supplement reports 0.31505 without restating a formula. Smoothing improves the squared statistic, but 'closely approximates' should be tempered by roughly 51.5% relative field error under the displayed normalization.

key_findings.claim: The simplest learned PBP model agrees with a low-anisotropy kinetic closure because the supplement derives essentially the same two-term equation under that assumption.
key_findings.evidence: The learned polarization equation contains linear relaxation, density gradient, and rho times the phoretic gradient. Its coefficients -1.3 and -0.48 are near the low-anisotropy analytic values -1 and -0.5, with the fitted latent field absorbing the remaining prefactor. The supplement sets the second angular Fourier mode approximately to zero and derives dot w=-gradient rho/2-w+beta rho gradient c/2. The paper itself notes that agreement is therefore unsurprising in the small-drift regime; it validates support recovery inside a known closure class rather than revealing a previously unknown mechanism.

anchors.section: Supplement Table III and Section V / kinetic derivation

key_findings.claim: The deterministic PDEs intentionally average away finite-population fluctuations, so they are not validated stochastic coarse-grained models.
key_findings.evidence: The procedure assumes slowly varying mean fields and fits deterministic time derivatives. Noise enters only through stochastic microscopic simulators; the learned PDE has no fluctuation term, finite-size scaling, covariance model, or fluctuation-dissipation relation. The cell case explicitly restricts to low density fluctuations, and the PBP kinetic derivation assumes low anisotropy. This can be suitable in a macroscopic mean-field regime, but does not support mesoscopic flocks, rare transitions, uncertainty, or noise-driven collective phases.

key_findings.claim: Coarse-graining and differentiation are central sources of bias but receive no sensitivity or uncertainty analysis.
key_findings.evidence: Adaptive KDE starts from a manually chosen pilot bandwidth; reported global values are 1.5, 50 micrometers, and 0.5 for the three systems. Fields are sampled on fixed 100-by-100 grids, then differentiated to form both response and highly correlated candidate columns. The supplement does not specify the derivative estimator used to build the regression dictionary, and Figure 3 marks a spectral cutoff tied to the Gaussian bandwidth. No bandwidth sweep, grid-convergence test, derivative-error propagation, or boundary/kernel alternative is reported.

key_findings.claim: The vector-field normalization is ambiguous between the generic supplement and the cell-model definition.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement Equation 4 defines a coarse vector field as a raw kernel sum of particle vector properties, which has density-weighted units. That is appropriate for polarization density w. The main cell section instead defines u with a division by density to obtain a local mean velocity, while the simulation details only say coarse-grained velocity is approximated using KDE. The exact normalization and derivative pipeline are not released, and choosing momentum density versus mean velocity changes candidate scaling and coefficients.

key_findings.claim: The nonconvex optimizer and searched regularization path add unquantified algorithmic uncertainty.
key_findings.evidence: Equation 2 penalizes the number of active groups and is solved by gIHT using approximate proximal operators, so a global sparsest optimum is not guaranteed. Lambda ranges from 0.01 lambda_max to lambda_max, but grid resolution, initialization, stopping tolerance, convergence diagnostics, and coefficient refit details are absent here. Stability under data half-sampling can include repeated convergence to the same local algorithmic solution; it does not distinguish optimization stability from model identifiability.

key_findings.claim: The manuscript contains additional reproducibility-relevant notation defects beyond the damping sign.
key_findings.evidence: Supplement Figure 3 calls the microscopic crowding parameter lambda in panels A-B but gamma in panel D and the main text, colliding with lambda used for regression regularization. Trend-filtering Equation 11 prints a lower summation index j-1 rather than j=1. The PBP kinetic derivation writes sin(delta)=partial_y/|gradient c|, omitting c in the numerator. These are locally inferable typographical errors, but together with the damping contradiction they make code and exact parameters necessary for reliable reproduction.

key_findings.claim: The official paper artifact is insufficient to reproduce any reported inference or PDE-validation figure.
key_findings.evidence: The arXiv record has only v1 and exposes no target-specific code or data. The official 55-file source archive contains TeX, bibliography, compiled PDFs, and static figure files, but no simulation or inference code, particle trajectories, learned coefficients beyond tables, random seeds, environment, parameter files, or advertised Supplementary Video/movie. Generic OpenFPM and PDE-STRIDE implementations exist separately, but the target paper supplies no exact commands or active-matter adapters. Several results require undocumented random field realizations and sampling choices.

key_findings.claim: Later work broadens the validation frontier toward local mechanisms, stochastic mesoscopic equations, stable learned closures, parameter sweeps, experimental forces, and structure-preserving coarse-graining.
key_findings.evidence: Same-author work learns locally dominant force balances and releases a large code/data artifact; mesoscopic equation discovery retains population-size-dependent stochasticity; learned kinetic closures explicitly train for a-posteriori stability across parameter space; later spectral active-matter PDE discovery studies flocking and phase separation; experimental stochastic-force inference recovers general pair forces; and metriplectic learning enforces conservation, dissipation, and fluctuation-dissipation by construction. These successors show that support stability on one synthetic regime is only one part of trustworthy coarse-graining.

method.core_idea: Convert stochastic agent trajectories into smooth hydrodynamic fields, then use physically grouped sparse regression and stability selection to identify a small deterministic PDE support and spatially or state-varying coefficients that survive data perturbations.
method.mechanism: Adaptive kernel density estimation maps particle positions and vector properties to density, polarization, and velocity grids. Numerical time and space derivatives populate a response vector and hand-designed candidate library. Non-overlapping groups tie terms required by physical priors or the same term across density or spatial blocks. Group iterative hard thresholding approximately solves an L0-like penalized least-squares problem across a lambda path. About 100 random half-samples estimate inclusion frequencies, and a threshold derived from a target expected false-positive count defines stable supports. Coefficients are refit, with Laplacian trend filtering for varying fields. Learned PDEs are numerically integrated and compared with particle-derived supports, patterns, summary statistics, or selected trajectories.
assumptions: Slowly varying deterministic hydrodynamic fields are meaningful averages of the stochastic particle process.
The chosen density, polarity, and velocity variables form a sufficient Markovian continuum state.
Adaptive KDE bandwidths chosen manually preserve the relevant scales while suppressing microscopic noise.
Numerical derivatives of the smoothed fields are accurate enough for sparse support recovery.
The true sufficient PDE lies in the manually constructed scalar and vector dictionaries.
Physical priors can be represented by non-overlapping groups of dictionary columns.
A parsimonious support is preferable to a fuller kinetic equation when terms are exchangeable on observed data.
gIHT's approximate nonconvex solution path finds the relevant supports consistently.
Random half-samples of correlated space-time rows satisfy stability-selection assumptions well enough for nominal false-positive control.
Recovery somewhere along a searched lambda path is a useful proxy for statistical consistency.
Density bins and shared-support groups correctly express state-dependent transport coefficients.
A Laplacian trend prior is appropriate for the hidden phoretic gradient field.
The SPP regimes, low-density-fluctuation cell model, and low-anisotropy PBP model are representative validation settings.
Matching selected pattern speeds, stationary statistics, and point trajectories is sufficient validation of the deterministic closure.
Finite-size stochastic fluctuations and memory can be neglected for the target phenomena.

techniques.role: Maps particle locations and properties onto smooth density, polarization, and velocity fields.
Enumerates symmetry- and domain-informed scalar and vector PDE candidates.
Approximately solves a nonconvex group-L0 penalized regression across regularization values.
Uses repeated random half-samples to estimate term inclusion frequencies and choose supports.
Translates a desired expected false-positive count into a nominal selection threshold.
Measures rediscovery of a chosen signed support somewhere along the lambda path as sample size grows.
Stacks density- or location-specific dictionaries and groups corresponding terms to learn varying coefficients.
Refits selected varying coefficients under a Laplacian L1 smoothness penalty using ADMM.
Compares learned supports and coefficients with available active-matter kinetic closures.
Integrates learned PDEs with finite differences and compares emergent patterns or summary statistics.
Withholds a known smooth phoretic field while supplying symmetry-compatible latent-gradient candidate groups.

evaluations.setting: Self-propelled particles near the Vicsek limit with 3,000 particles, 10 density candidates, and 14 polarization candidates.
evaluations.metric: Stability plots, nominal expected false positives, signed-support recovery over 20 trials, and coefficient comparison with kinetic theory.
evaluations.result: The continuity support and two sparse polarization supports become increasingly recoverable with row sample size; the fuller kinetic support remains unrecoverable at the stated threshold because terms are exchangeable.
evaluations.baseline: An analytical kinetic support on the same simulated regime; no alternative PDE-discovery algorithm or independent trajectory split.

evaluations.setting: SPP lane formation at low crowding and density-dependent motility at three gamma values.
evaluations.metric: Average lane speed and MSE of inferred normalized speed versus density.
evaluations.result: S1,rho plus S2,w produces lanes near the particle speed of 2.1; grouped density blocks track the known exponential motility curve with plotted MSE between about 0.0001 and 0.0026.
evaluations.baseline: Kinetic-theory PDE and the generating particle simulation at the same parameters; no held-out phase or parameter regime.

evaluations.setting: A 4,000-particle stochastic epithelial-cell simulator calibrated to prior experimental velocity statistics.
evaluations.metric: Support recovery, velocity-magnitude distribution, velocity power spectrum, and velocity correlation function.
evaluations.result: Two deterministic PDE supports are selected; the cubic model is said to be numerically stable and both reproduce selected summary statistics over resolved scales.
evaluations.baseline: The same stochastic simulator, initialized into the PDE; no raw epithelial experiment, field forecast, independent seed band, or transfer test.

evaluations.setting: Internal audit of the two learned cell PDEs and their supplementary coefficient table.
evaluations.metric: Consistency of support membership, coefficient sign, and claimed amplitude damping.
evaluations.result: The text says S2 both lacks and contains the cubic term; the table prints +0.008 although damping with +2.7 linear growth requires a negative cubic. A commented official-source line gives -0.008, identifying the rendered sign error.
evaluations.baseline: The manuscript's own Table II, paragraph, source TeX, and the spatially uniform-mode dynamics.

evaluations.setting: Phoretic Brownian particles with 5,000 agents, beta=0.3, one smooth random Fourier forcing field, and low anisotropy.
evaluations.metric: Selected support, fitted coefficients, latent-gradient field error, and density/polarization trajectories at two points.
evaluations.result: The learned simple closure approximates analytic coefficients and trajectories; the field's reported squared relative error is 0.2654 after smoothing versus 0.31505 without it.
evaluations.baseline: A kinetic-theory model, the same particle simulation, and the known withheld field; only one forcing realization and parameter regime.

evaluations.setting: Low-anisotropy kinetic derivation for the PBP model.
evaluations.result: Setting the second angular Fourier mode to zero gives dot w=-gradient rho/2-w+beta rho gradient c/2, essentially the selected S1,w support.
evaluations.baseline: The fuller analytical closure SA,w; no test outside low drift and low anisotropy.

evaluations.setting: Coarse-graining and numerical implementation across all three simulated systems.
evaluations.metric: Specified particle counts, grids, KDE bandwidths, time steps, and PDE summary plots.
evaluations.result: The supplement gives major simulator and solver parameters, but omits derivative construction, seeds, realized forcing coefficients, regularization grids, gIHT tolerances, and sensitivity analyses.
evaluations.baseline: No bandwidth, grid, differentiation, or optimizer ablation.

evaluations.setting: Official arXiv v1 record and source archive audited on 2026-08-23.
evaluations.metric: Presence of runnable code, data, configurations, random seeds, outputs, and advertised media.
evaluations.result: The 55-file archive contains manuscript sources and static figures only; there is no target inference/simulation code, trajectory data, environment, seeds, or Supplementary Video/movie.
evaluations.baseline: Generic external OpenFPM and PDE-STRIDE projects exist but are not packaged into a target reproduction route.

limitations: The central algorithmic components substantially predate this active-matter application.
All three inference studies use synthetic particle simulations rather than raw experimental trajectories.
The cell simulator is calibrated to experiments, but the learned PDE is not validated on epithelial imaging data.
Candidate hydrodynamic variables, PDE terms, symmetries, dependency covariate, and latent-field products are supplied by the analyst.
A true term absent from the dictionary cannot be recovered or diagnosed.
Group-IHT optimization is nonconvex and only approximately solved.
Random space-time rows are correlated through particle dynamics, KDE support, and derivative stencils.
Nominal false-positive control assumptions are not checked or empirically calibrated.
Recovery probability is relative to a selected support and permits success at any lambda, not recovery of known truth under a fixed procedure.
The SPP analytical support is not identifiable because candidate terms are exchangeable on the observed regime.
KDE bandwidths are manually chosen and no sensitivity or uncertainty analysis is shown.
The numerical differentiation method used for inference is not specified in this paper.
Vector KDE normalization is ambiguous for the cell velocity field.
PDE validation largely reuses generating regimes, initial fields, and selected summary statistics.
There are no independent initial-condition, geometry, parameter, particle-count, or phase holdouts.
The deterministic PDEs omit finite-population fluctuations, memory, rare events, and stochastic forcing.
The cell model is explicitly restricted to low density fluctuations and the PBP closure to low anisotropy.
The hidden phoretic field is one deterministic smooth low-frequency realization with a supplied smoothness prior.
The field metric called RMSE is actually a squared-norm ratio and corresponds to about 51.5% relative L2 error.
The cell damping paragraph contradicts its table, and the table omits the minus sign needed for stability.
Several supplement equations and captions contain additional index, symbol, and derivative typos.
No target-specific code, data, seeds, environment, or advertised supplementary movie is distributed in the official record.
The arXiv manuscript remained at v1, so the internal contradictions were never corrected there.
failure_modes: A user-chosen dictionary excludes the true closure term, causing a stable but physically wrong surrogate support.
Correlated candidate terms exchange support across samples, making a simpler sufficient model look uniquely recovered.
Random row subsampling treats dependent space-time observations as independent and understates selection uncertainty.
gIHT converges repeatedly to the same local support, which stability selection mistakes for model identifiability.
A coarse KDE bandwidth erases short-scale physics or changes derivative coefficients and spectral validation.
A fine bandwidth amplifies particle noise and makes derivative columns unstable.
Density bin width or smoothness strength imposes the shape of a variable coefficient more strongly than the data.
A latent field outside the low-frequency smooth class is absorbed into wrong PDE terms or over-smoothed.
A deterministic closure matches stationary spectra while failing transient, rare-event, or finite-size stochastic behavior.
A support-stable PDE is numerically ill posed, as the unstable cell model illustrates.
A sign transcription error converts cubic damping into finite-time growth and prevents reproduction.
Momentum density and mean velocity are confused by an undocumented normalization choice.
Validation on the same simulator, parameter regime, and initial field hides poor extrapolation across active-matter phases.
reusable_insights: Separate prior consistency, selection stability, structural correctness, numerical well-posedness, and predictive transfer as distinct validation layers.
Use trajectory- or simulation-level blocked resampling when particle-derived space-time rows are correlated.
Calibrate stability-selection false-positive bounds empirically under the actual dependency structure.
Pre-register hydrodynamic variables, dictionary terms, group structure, and lambda selection before inspecting target outcomes.
Compare multiple derivative and coarse-graining operators and propagate their uncertainty into support frequencies.
Test learned PDEs across independent seeds, initial conditions, particle counts, parameters, geometries, and phases.
Retain stochastic terms when finite-size effects or noise-driven transitions are part of the target phenomenon.
Report field trajectory errors and conserved quantities in addition to stationary marginal spectra and correlations.
Audit coefficient signs with dimensional analysis, uniform-mode stability, and executable unit tests.
Treat hidden-field recovery as conditional on an explicit field class and quantify sensitivity to smoothness strength and spatial frequency.
Release exact particle trajectories, coarse fields, derivative matrices, regularization paths, seeds, and PDE solver configs.
Use exact analytical closures as falsification tests while acknowledging when observed data make their terms non-identifiable.
open_questions: Can stability-selection guarantees be extended or calibrated for KDE-smoothed, stencil-correlated particle data?
How should one jointly learn the coarse variables, kernel bandwidth, PDE support, and closure memory instead of fixing the first two?
Can a method diagnose that no equation in its candidate library is sufficient?
What blocked experimental design most efficiently separates exchangeable convective active-matter terms?
How do support and coefficients change across particle number, density, alignment, noise, and phase transitions?
When is a deterministic mean-field PDE adequate, and when is a stochastic PDE or generalized Langevin closure necessary?
Can hidden drift fields be recovered across unseen spectra, discontinuities, temporal variation, and multiple simultaneous latent causes?
What is the correct uncertainty interval for a learned varying coefficient after both support selection and trend filtering?
Can numerical stability and conservation be enforced during support selection rather than checked after fitting?
Would weak-form derivatives improve robustness and reduce dependence on KDE bandwidth for raw particle trajectories?
Can the cell PDE be validated prospectively on real epithelial movies and perturbations rather than a calibrated particle simulator?
Do the intended negative cubic coefficient and unavailable original code reproduce Figure 3 exactly?

competitive_landscape.title: Discovering governing equations from data: Sparse identification of nonlinear dynamical systems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Foundational sparse-identification predecessor establishing parsimonious equation discovery from candidate libraries.
competitive_landscape.difference: It focuses mainly on low-dimensional dynamics and fluid-mode models; the target applies grouped support selection to particle-derived PDE fields.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven discovery of partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct PDE-FIND predecessor using sparse regression over nonlinear and derivative libraries.
competitive_landscape.difference: It starts from measured continuum fields and Pareto model selection; the target adds particle coarse-graining, physical groups, and stability selection.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning Dynamical Systems and Bifurcation via Group Sparsity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Group-sparse equation-learning predecessor tying model support across datasets and bifurcation parameters.
competitive_landscape.difference: It provides convergence analysis for parameterized dynamical systems rather than spatially coarse-grained active-particle PDEs.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven identification of parametric partial differential equations
competitive_landscape.relationship: Close predecessor using group sparsity to identify PDE terms with arbitrary space- or time-dependent coefficients.
competitive_landscape.difference: It works from continuum simulations with group thresholded regression; the target adapts variable coefficients to density blocks and microscopic trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning force fields from stochastic trajectories
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct stochastic-trajectory predecessor estimating deterministic forces, diffusion, currents, and inference error.
competitive_landscape.difference: It learns microscopic stochastic force fields with information-theoretic uncertainty rather than deterministic macroscopic PDE supports.

competitive_landscape.title: DeepMoD: Deep learning for Model Discovery in noisy data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Neural PDE-discovery predecessor designed for sparse and noisy measurements.
competitive_landscape.difference: A neural surrogate supplies smooth automatic derivatives and sparse regression; the target instead KDE-smooths particle data and enforces grouped physical priors.

competitive_landscape.title: Stability selection enables robust learning of partial differential equations from limited noisy data
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-author direct methodological predecessor introducing PDE-STRIDE, iterative hard thresholding, stability plots, and achievability analysis.
competitive_landscape.difference: It benchmarks continuum PDE recovery and real microscopy; the target reuses the selection machinery for cross-scale active-particle fields and groups.

competitive_landscape.title: Using Noisy or Incomplete Data to Discover Models of Spatiotemporal Dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Close weak-form predecessor handling high derivatives, strong noise, incomplete observations, and latent pressure or forcing fields.
competitive_landscape.difference: It avoids pointwise derivative amplification and reconstructs hidden fluid variables from experimental fields; the target uses KDE and grouped latent-gradient coefficients from particle simulations.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning the Non-Equilibrium Dynamics of Brownian Movies
competitive_landscape.relationship: Stochastic experimental-data predecessor learning dissipative modes, forces, currents, and entropy production from Brownian movies.
competitive_landscape.difference: It retains mesoscopic stochastic dynamics in a learned reduced basis, whereas the target averages into deterministic hydrodynamic PDEs.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning physically consistent mathematical models from data using group sparsity
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-author immediate predecessor providing gIHT, non-overlapping physical groups, stability selection, varying coefficients, and latent-variable examples.
competitive_landscape.difference: The target's algorithm is largely this framework applied to microscopic active-particle coarse-graining rather than a new optimizer or consistency theory.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning hydrodynamic equations for active matter from particle simulations and experiments
competitive_landscape.relationship: Closest direct predecessor learning symmetry-aware active-matter PDEs from both particle simulations and microroller experiments.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses spectral representations and sparse regression with a specialized design and includes experimental validation; the target emphasizes generic group priors, stability selection, variable coefficients, and a hidden field.

competitive_landscape.title: Robust learning from noisy, incomplete, high-dimensional experimental data via physically constrained symbolic regression
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct predecessor for physics-constrained PDE discovery with inaccessible pressure and forcing fields.
competitive_landscape.difference: It uses weak formulations on a turbulent fluid experiment, while the target uses grouped pointwise libraries on synthetic active-particle trajectories.

competitive_landscape.title: A Data-Driven Statistical Description for the Hydrodynamics of Active Matter
competitive_landscape.relationship: Contemporary active-matter competitor inferring phase-space statistics and a field theory from simulated and bacterial-swarm experimental data.
competitive_landscape.difference: It targets stochastic statistical descriptions and near-steady field theories rather than a sparse deterministic PDE support from particle derivatives.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning stochastic dynamics and predicting emergent behavior using transformers
competitive_landscape.relationship: Near-concurrent alternative learning microscopic active-matter transition rules from one stochastic trajectory and extrapolating an unseen phase transition.
competitive_landscape.difference: It is less interpretable and does not produce a hydrodynamic PDE, but retains stochastic rules and tests density transfer that the target does not.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven discovery of stochastic dynamical equations of collective motion
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct successor learning mesoscopic stochastic equations and population-size scaling for self-propelled collective motion.
competitive_landscape.difference: It retains multiplicative finite-flock noise and studies density and interaction-radius deviations from mean field, beyond the target's deterministic macroscopic closure.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning locally dominant force balances in active particle systems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-author successor combining clustering and sparse inference to identify phase-local mechanisms in bands and asters.
competitive_landscape.difference: It resolves spatially local dominant balances and releases a large code/data artifact, addressing heterogeneity and reproducibility absent from the target.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning fast, accurate, and stable closures of a kinetic theory of an active fluid
competitive_landscape.relationship: Same-first-author successor explicitly learning closure functions for active-fluid kinetic theory.
competitive_landscape.difference: It trains symmetry-aware neural closures for a-priori accuracy and a-posteriori stability across parameter space, directly addressing closure stability and transfer rather than only sparse support.

competitive_landscape.title: Physics-informed AI and ML-based sparse system identification algorithm for discovery of PDE's representing nonlinear dynamic systems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Modern PDE-discovery competitor targeting noisy, stiff, high-order, and correlated candidate systems.
competitive_landscape.difference: It combines spline derivatives, denoising, correlated-term removal, and physics-informed refinement; the target uses KDE derivatives and does not explicitly resolve correlated columns.

competitive_landscape.title: Estimation of spatial and time scales of collective behaviors of active matters through learning hydrodynamic equations from particle dynamics
competitive_landscape.relationship: Direct current successor using coarse-graining, spectral representations, and sparse regression for Vicsek and active Brownian particles.
competitive_landscape.difference: It emphasizes characteristic spatial and temporal scales and validates flocking and phase separation across two active-matter models, rather than variable coefficients and hidden fields.

competitive_landscape.title: Learning general pair interactions between self-propelled particles
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current experimental successor using stochastic force inference on flocking and disordered Janus-particle trajectories.
competitive_landscape.difference: It recovers radial, angular, transverse, and torque interactions with uncertainty and validates simulations across density, rather than fitting a deterministic continuum PDE.

competitive_landscape.title: Data-driven particle dynamics: Structure-preserving coarse-graining for emergent behavior in non-equilibrium systems
competitive_landscape.relationship: Current structure-preserving coarse-graining successor for nonequilibrium particle trajectories and colloidal video.
competitive_landscape.difference: Its metriplectic construction enforces discrete conservation, dissipation, momentum, and fluctuation-dissipation while learning latent structural variables, retaining stochastic thermodynamic structure absent from the target.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: A generic statistical-learning framework with physical group priors can robustly and consistently learn deterministic hydrodynamic equations, spatially or state-varying coefficients, and latent drift fields directly from stochastic active-particle trajectories.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper applies adaptive particle coarse-graining, gIHT, stability selection, block-grouped coefficient functions, smooth latent-field regression, and PDE simulation to three active-particle systems. It recovers selected supports consistent with kinetic theory, reproduces one SPP lane speed, matches cell velocity summary statistics, and reconstructs a low-frequency phoretic field and PBP point trajectories.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The strongest novelty is a useful integration and application: group-stable sparse PDE discovery across microscopic stochastic simulations and macroscopic active-matter fields, with demonstrations of density-dependent coefficients and a latent gradient. The core optimizer, stability analysis, variable-coefficient grouping, latent-variable idea, and particle-to-active-hydrodynamic learning all have direct predecessors. 'Guaranteeing' physical consistency and statistical robustness is too broad because priors are manually encoded, correlated space-time resampling is not validated, recovery is relative to chosen supports, one stable support is numerically unstable, and there is no experimental or cross-regime holdout. Damping and metric inconsistencies plus the absence of code/data prevent exact reproduction. Later stochastic, local, stable-closure, experimental-force, and structure-preserving successors materially advance the validation standard.

reviewer_notes: Read all 13 pages of the canonical arXiv v1 PDF and exact cached text, including the seven-page supplement, all equations, tables, references, and every visual panel in main Figures 1-4 and supplementary Figures 1-4; rendered and inspected every page at original resolution with no missing figure pixels. Audited support definitions and all printed transport-coefficient tables. Confirmed the cell paragraph literally says S2,u both lacks and is stabilized by u|u|^2; confirmed Supplement Table II prints +8e-3, while the official source contains a commented simulation line with -0.008, so the published sign is not a matter of qualitative interpretation. Recomputed the uniform-mode sign logic and sqrt(0.2654)=0.5152 for the field metric. Inspected the exact official arXiv source archive: 55 files consisting of TeX, bibliography, compiled manuscript material, and static figures; no code, particle data, configs, seeds, environment, or referenced video/movie. Confirmed v1 is the only arXiv revision and no target-specific artifact is linked. Checked 21 primary-paper predecessors and successors through 2026-08-23, especially PDE-FIND, parametric and stability-selected group sparsity, weak-form hidden-field recovery, direct active-matter hydrodynamic learning, stochastic mesoscopic discovery, stable learned closures, experimental force inference, and structure-preserving coarse-graining.
